name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court legally imposed the mandatory minimum fine by suspending the portion the defendant could not pay, harmonizing statutory provisions and overruling Gibbons' facial unconstitutionality holding.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Concurred, argued that Gibbons' holding that the mandatory minimum fine was facially unconstitutional was a significant error and the current opinion corrects it.

name: Justice Katherine M. Bidegaray
description: Dissented, argued that the mandatory minimum fine is unconstitutional regardless of suspension, and that the court should have severed the unconstitutional minimum floor instead of rewriting statutes.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, argued that the mandatory minimum fine is unconstitutional regardless of suspension, and that the court should have severed the unconstitutional minimum floor instead of rewriting statutes.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the mandatory minimum fine is unconstitutional regardless of suspension, and that the court should have severed the unconstitutional minimum floor instead of rewriting statutes.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, argued that the State Policies likely result in unequal treatment and discrimination based on sex, violating Article II, Section 4 of the Montana Constitution, and that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in granting the preliminary injunction.

name: Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the preliminary injunction should be upheld to preserve the status quo, finding strict scrutiny appropriate for the infringement of a fundamental right to individual dignity and privacy, and that the State cannot constitutionally deny citizens the opportunity to obtain accurate identification documents.

name: Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the court forces the State to issue falsified legal documents by conflating biological sex with gender identity, that transgender individuals do not constitute a suspect class, and that the District Court applied the wrong legal standard for the preliminary injunction.

name: CORY J. SWANSON
description: Dissented, argued that the court engaged in judicial law-making by intruding on the legislative and executive branches' policy-making authority, failed to establish standing for the MVD policy, and abused judicial power by striking down a statute and rule.

name: Katherine M. Bidegaray
description: Concurred, argued that BI-8 constitutes a single constitutional amendment and the Attorney General lacked statutory authority to append a fiscal statement.

name: Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the restriction on government influence or the use of government resources is an additional express constitutional change, unrelated to the ballot issue approval process, and thus violates the separate-vote requirement.

name: Cory J. Swanson
description: Dissented, argued that BI-8 impermissibly amends the judicial power and the constitutional rights of litigants to access courts and due process by imposing inflexible, date-certain deadlines for resolving legal challenges, constituting multiple, unrelated amendments.

name: Chief Justice Cory J. Swanson
description: Concurred, argued that Knudsen violated Rules 3.4(c) and 5.1(c) but the case should be dismissed due to the Commission's due process violations, and that the Attorney General is subject to professional conduct rules but the rules cannot be used as a political tool.

name: District Court Judge Jessica T. Fehr
District Court Judge Gregory L. Bonilla
District Court Judge Paul Sullivan
description: Concurred, argued that prudential considerations and procedural deficiencies warranted dismissal without reaching the substantive question of whether Knudsen's conduct warranted discipline, emphasizing institutional limits and judicial restraint.

name: Justice Katherine M. Bidegaray
description: Dissented from the dismissal, arguing that Knudsen's conduct in disobeying court orders was prejudicial to the administration of justice (Rule 8.4(d)), that procedural irregularities did not violate due process or cause substantial prejudice, and that meaningful discipline (public censure and 30-day suspension) was warranted to uphold the rule of law and professional accountability.

name: Jim Rice
description: Concurred, argued that the mandatory minimum custodial sentence for felony DUI is constitutional and not disproportionate to the crime, distinguishing it from mandatory fines.

name: Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the MLUPA's public participation provisions are not facially unconstitutional and the housing reform laws do not violate equal protection, and vacated the ruling on restrictive covenants as an advisory opinion.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred, argued that the Attorney General's revised statement was misleading and did not fairly state what was proposed, and that MNC's proposed statement was compliant.

name: Chief Justice Cory J. Swanson
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that both the Attorney General's and MNC's ballot statements were inadequate and should be remanded for revision.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the Attorney General's revised statement was legally adequate and should have been upheld, and that MNC's proposed statement was legally inadequate.

name: Beth Baker
description: Concurred, arguing that a rational juror could determine Doman's activity interfered with the traffic stop and obstructed officers' duties, and his constitutional challenges were not properly preserved for appeal.

name: JAMES JEREMIAH SHEA
description: Concurred, highlighting Officer Minaglia's professionalism in handling the encounter, noting that the right to film was not disputed, but Doman's failure to preserve constitutional arguments meant the case was solely about sufficiency of evidence for obstruction.

name: JAMES JEREMIAH SHEA
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court did not rely on clearly erroneous findings of fact when it denied Herzog's motion to suppress, as Detective Holzer had sufficient particularized suspicion for the stop based on the totality of circumstances.

name: KATHERINE M BIDEGARAY
description: Concurred, argued that while the totality of circumstances justified the investigatory stop under current Montana law, courts must exercise caution in broadly interpreting seemingly innocuous conduct as grounds for particularized suspicion to avoid diluting constitutional protections.

name: CORY J. SWANSON
description: Concurred with Justice Bidegaray's concurring opinion.

name: BETH BAKER
description: Concurred with Justice Bidegaray's concurring opinion.

name: LAURIE MCKINNON
description: Concurred with Justice Bidegaray's concurring opinion.

name: INGRID GUSTAFSON
description: Concurred with Justice Bidegaray's concurring opinion.

name: JIM RICE
description: Concurred with Justice Bidegaray's concurring opinion.

name: Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court properly cured its procedural error and correctly dismissed Netzer's constitutional claims, and that HB 702's title was sufficiently clear to uphold both Subsection (1) and Subsection (4) under the Montana Constitution's clear-title requirement.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, delivered the opinion establishing a presumption for attorney's fees in right-to-know cases and also wrote separately to address the dissents' attacks on the Court's integrity.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred, argued that providing guidance for attorney's fees in right-to-know cases is well-precedented and necessary to ensure constitutional rights are enforceable.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Dissented, argued that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in denying attorney's fees and that a presumption for fees is inappropriate given the need to balance competing rights.

name: Chief Justice Cory J. Swanson
description: Dissented, joined Justice Baker's and Justice Rice's dissents, and emphasized his duty to interpret laws and the Constitution, even if it means disagreeing with colleagues.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's new presumption lacks legal basis and reflects a trend of the Court setting aside established legal principles in favor of policy preferences.

name: BETH BAKER, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that DEQ's noise analysis was not arbitrary or capricious, DEQ failed to take a "hard look" at lighting impacts, MEPA requires DEQ to analyze greenhouse gas emissions, and the District Court erred in vacating the permit without specific findings.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Concurred, argued that the vacatur of the permit should be reversed because the case is moot as the plant is operational, and DEQ's initial decision not to conduct GHG analysis was an informed discretionary determination.

name: Justice Dirk Sandefur
description: Concurred, joining Justice Jim Rice's special concurring opinion.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the Court undermined MEPA's significance in protecting environmental rights and failed to provide an effective remedy by reversing the permit's vacatur despite finding MEPA violations.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, joining Justice Laurie McKinnon's special concurring opinion and dissent.

name: Jim Rice
description: Concurred, argued that DNRC's interpretation of the MWUA is correct and constitutional, as mine dewatering for disposal is neither a beneficial use nor waste under the Act, and the Act's purpose is to regulate water rights, not the water resource itself.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred, argued that Appellants (MTU) do have standing to challenge DNRC's permitting decision based on their recreational and aesthetic interests in publicly-owned water rights.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that mine dewatering is a beneficial use requiring a permit under the MWUA, that the Court's interpretation creates an unconstitutional loophole, and that the DNRC's policy is inconsistent with statutory language and legislative intent to protect Montana's water resources.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, joined Justice Laurie McKinnon's dissenting opinion.

name: MIKE MCGRATH
description: Concurred, argued that the Legislature may explicitly prohibit local government units with self-government powers from exercising certain powers, and that local initiative power is subject to the same rules as local government units.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the statute unconstitutionally restricts the people's reserved power of initiative, which should not be curtailed when citizens seek to regulate auxiliary containers.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, argued that the statute unconstitutionally restricts the people's reserved power of initiative, which should not be curtailed when citizens seek to regulate auxiliary containers.

name: James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred, argued that Montana law recognizes a gubernatorial privilege rooted in the state's constitutional history, necessary for the integrity of government, but subject to strict parameters and in camera review.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that no executive or gubernatorial privilege should be recognized under Montana law, as it is unnecessary and an affront to the Constitution's emphasis on open government and the public's right to know.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, argued that no executive or gubernatorial privilege should be recognized under Montana law, as it is unnecessary and an affront to the Constitution's emphasis on open government and the public's right to know.

name: Leslie Halligan
description: Dissented, argued that no executive or gubernatorial privilege should be recognized under Montana law, as it is unnecessary and an affront to the Constitution's emphasis on open government and the public's right to know.

name: Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the challenged laws violate Montana's constitutional rights to privacy, equal protection, and free speech by infringing on personal and procreative autonomy without a compelling, medically acknowledged health risk.

name: Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the court's absolutist application of the right to privacy fails to account for the State's vital role in protecting human life, that the constitutional history does not support an abortion right, and that the challenged laws should not be dismissed as entirely unconstitutional.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court did not manifestly abuse its discretion or commit an error of law in granting a preliminary injunction against SB 99, based on the plaintiffs' likelihood of success on their right to privacy claim.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, argued that the Court should have also addressed the plaintiffs' equal protection claim, as transgender discrimination is sex discrimination and triggers strict scrutiny.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, argued that the Court should have also addressed the plaintiffs' equal protection claim, as transgender discrimination is sex discrimination and triggers strict scrutiny.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Concurred with the injunction on medical restrictions but dissented on enjoining the funding prohibition, arguing funding decisions should be subject to rational basis review.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, arguing that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in granting the preliminary injunction, as the challenged provisions likely infringe on the constitutional rights to privacy and equal protection.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, arguing that the Court's decision was correct in its entirety and that the Court was required to address both privacy and equal protection claims to provide clear guidance.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Concurred, arguing that the District Court correctly applied strict scrutiny to privacy claims, but the Court should have exercised judicial restraint and not addressed equal protection issues at this preliminary stage.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred with Justice Beth Baker's special concurrence.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, arguing that the challenged bills concern government healthcare funding, not medical procedures, and should be assessed under rational basis review, not strict scrutiny, and that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court did not manifestly abuse its discretion by granting a preliminary injunction against HB 575 and HB 721, as the Providers are likely to succeed on the merits, would suffer irreparable harm, and the injunction is in the public interest.

name: JIM RICE
description: Concurred with enjoining HB 721, arguing that the State failed to prove a medically acknowledged health risk. Dissented from enjoining HB 575, arguing that the District Court's analysis was flawed by not recognizing the State's compelling interest in ensuring pre-viability abortions and the presumption of constitutionality for HB 575, which uses a recognized medical procedure (ultrasound) to determine gestational age.

name: MIKE MCGRATH
description: Concurred, delivered the opinion of the court, finding that the Secretary's fees for the voter file are lawful and do not violate the constitutional 'right to know' as ACORN's request was not specific enough.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred, argued that the warrantless entry was justified under the community caretaker doctrine due to exigent circumstances and that no Brady violation occurred.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the Court's analysis is confusing, misapprehends Caniglia, and incorrectly extends the community caretaker doctrine to warrantless home entries without sufficient probable cause or exigent circumstances.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, joining Justice McKinnon's dissent, arguing that the Court's analysis is confusing, misapprehends Caniglia, and incorrectly extends the community caretaker doctrine to warrantless home entries without sufficient probable cause or exigent circumstances.

name: Justice Dirk Sandefur
description: Dissented, joining Justice McKinnon's dissent, arguing that the Court's analysis is confusing, misapprehends Caniglia, and incorrectly extends the community caretaker doctrine to warrantless home entries without sufficient probable cause or exigent circumstances.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, argued that the Consent Act violates a minor's fundamental right to privacy and equal protection under the Montana Constitution.

name: Jim Rice
description: Concurred with the ultimate holdings that the Consent Act violates privacy and equal protection, but disagreed with the majority's equal protection analysis and clarified prior holdings regarding minors' rights.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred, argued that the Montana Constitution's right to a clean and healthful environment includes a stable climate system and that the MEPA Limitation is unconstitutional for preventing the analysis of GHG emissions.

name: Justice Dirk Sandefur
description: Concurred, argued that the right to a stable climate system is included in the clean and healthful environment, and that the legislative attempts to pare back MEPA review are unconstitutional, but questioned the lack of particularized causation evidence.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing because their injury was abstract and indistinguishable from the general public, and the MEPA Limitation alone did not cause the alleged injury or provide redress.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred, arguing that the Attorney General erred in concluding the ballot issue was legally insufficient as its components were closely related and did not violate the separate-vote requirement.

name: Mike McGrath, Chief Justice
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court abused its discretion by denying attorney fees under the private attorney general doctrine, as the Legislature acted in bad faith by passing an unconstitutional bill with willful disregard for constitutional obligations, and the Appellants vindicated important constitutional interests.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the Court's reasoning for applying the private attorney general doctrine lacks merit under precedent, and the District Court did not abuse its discretion by denying fees, as the case was a 'garden variety' constitutional challenge not deserving of attorney fees.

name: Justice Dirk Sandefur
description: Dissented, argued that he joins in the dissenting opinion of Justice Rice.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred with the majority opinion on standing and the unconstitutionality of the bills, but dissented on the denial of attorney fees, arguing that fees should have been awarded due to the vindication of important constitutional interests and the State's concession of unconstitutionality for two bills.

name: Mike McGrath
description: Concurred with the majority opinion on standing and the unconstitutionality of the bills, and concurred with the denial of attorney fees, arguing that the equitable factors for awarding fees were not met and the District Court did not abuse its discretion.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred with the majority opinion on standing and the unconstitutionality of the bills, but dissented on the denial of attorney fees, arguing that fees should have been awarded due to the vindication of important constitutional interests and the State's concession of unconstitutionality for two bills.

name: James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred with the majority opinion on standing and the unconstitutionality of the bills, and concurred with the denial of attorney fees, arguing that the District Court did not abuse its discretion as it was not necessary for plaintiffs to initiate the action.

name: Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the legislation because the Board of Regents is the sole entity with exclusive constitutional authority over the university system.

name: Dirk M. Sandefur
description: Dissented, argued that the plaintiffs lacked jurisprudential standing to challenge the legislation as an infringement of the Board of Regents' constitutional authority.

name: LAURIE MCKINNON JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that the mandatory minimum fine statute is facially unconstitutional because it prevents courts from considering proportionality factors like ability to pay, violating the right against excessive fines.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Dissented, argued that the mandatory fine statute could be harmonized with the general sentencing statute to allow for ability-to-pay considerations without declaring it unconstitutional.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the mandatory fine statute is constitutional, distinguishable from prior invalidated statutes, and the Court's decision unnecessarily overturns precedent and is overbroad.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Dissented, joined Justice Rice's dissenting opinion.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, argued that the Attorney General's ballot statement was argumentative, inaccurate, and prejudicial, and that the court must intervene to ensure a clear and impartial ballot statement for voters.

name: MIKE MCGRATH CHIEF JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court abused its discretion by denying attorney fees under the private attorney general doctrine, as the unconstitutional sections of the bill were adopted through willful disregard of constitutional obligations and legislative rules.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, argued that the District Court did not abuse its discretion by denying fees, as the private attorney general doctrine should be invoked sparingly and the case did not warrant fees under precedent.

name: Dirk Sandefur
description: Dissented, argued that the District Court did not abuse its discretion by denying fees, as the private attorney general doctrine should be invoked sparingly and the case did not warrant fees under precedent.

name: LAURIE McKINNON
description: Concurred, joining Justice Gustafson's opinion that strict scrutiny, not middle-tier scrutiny, should apply to HB 506 because it impermissibly interferes with the right to vote by eliminating predominant voting options for a subclass.

name: INGRID GUSTAFSON
description: Concurred, arguing that strict scrutiny, not middle-tier scrutiny, should apply to HB 506 because it impermissibly interferes with the right to vote by eliminating predominant voting options for a subclass.

name: Beth Baker
description: Dissented from the finding that HB 506 is unconstitutional, arguing that the plaintiffs did not meet their burden to establish facial invalidity and that the law imposes only a minimal burden on a narrow subset of voters, thus not interfering with the fundamental right to vote.

name: DIRK M. SANDEFUR
description: Dissented from the findings that HB 176, HB 530, and SB 169 are unconstitutional, arguing the court erroneously applied strict scrutiny based on false assertions about the Montana Constitution providing greater protection than the US Constitution and misapplied intermediate scrutiny, while concurring that HB 506 is unconstitutional.

name: JIM RICE
description: Dissented, joining Justice Sandefur's opinion that the court erroneously applied strict scrutiny to HB 176, HB 530, and SB 169 based on false assertions about constitutional protection and misapplied intermediate scrutiny.

name: Jim Rice Justice
description: Concurred, argued that BI2 proposed multiple, unrelated constitutional changes in a single measure, violating the separate-vote requirement of the Montana Constitution, and the Attorney General's determination was within his authority.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, argued that the school districts' mask policies did not implicate fundamental rights under the Montana Constitution and were rationally related to the legitimate government interest of stemming the spread of COVID-19.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, arguing that the amended SVORA is punitive and its retroactive application violates the ex post facto clause.

name: DIRK M. SANDEFUR, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the post-2007 SVORA is punitive and violates the ex post facto law, and would overrule Mount.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred with the result, but argued that retroactive SVORA application violates the constitutional guarantee of full rights restoration and would overrule Mount on that basis.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, arguing that the SVORA is constitutional as a nonpunitive civil regulatory scheme and should be upheld.

name: DIRK SANDEFUR
description: Concurred, arguing that the District Court erroneously denied Noli's motion to suppress because the traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged and expanded into an unrelated drug investigation without objective particularized suspicion.

name: LAURIE MCKINNON
description: Concurred, argued that the State failed to demonstrate a medically acknowledged health risk to justify restricting abortion care by APRNs, thus infringing on a woman's fundamental right to privacy to choose her healthcare provider.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, arguing that the statute unconstitutionally violates the right to equal protection of the law for parents and children subject to dependent-neglect proceedings under ICWA by denying them prompt emergency protective services hearings.

name: BETH BAKER
description: Concurred, argued that the minute entries were not testimonial hearsay and their admission did not violate the Confrontation Clause, and the denial of the continuance was not an abuse of discretion.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the minute entries were testimonial hearsay, violating the confrontation right, and the error was not harmless; also joined Justice Shea's dissent on the continuance issue.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Dissented, argued that the trial court abused its discretion by denying the motion to continue, which prejudiced the defendant's substantial rights.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, argued that the trial court abused its discretion by denying the motion to continue, which prejudiced the defendant's substantial rights.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, arguing that the group home manager was not a state actor and had authority to confiscate the electronics based on group home rules Larson had consented to, thus the evidence was lawfully obtained.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Concurred, arguing that the warrantless search of Mefford's phone exceeded the scope of his consent and was not justified by the probation search exception, thus violating constitutional rights.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Dissented, arguing that while the search exceeded consent, it was a permissible probation search based on reasonable suspicion from the totality of circumstances, and the evidence should not be suppressed.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Dissented, joining Justice Shea's opinion that the search was a permissible probation search.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, joining Justice Shea's opinion that the search was a permissible probation search.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred, argued that HB 325 is facially unconstitutional based on binding judicial precedent (Reichert) and would deny Montanans their constitutional right to vote for Supreme Court justices, making the issue ripe for review.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Dissented, argued that the case was not ripe for judicial review because it lacked the immediate temporal urgency and threat of disenfranchisement present in the precedent case (Reichert).

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Dissented, joining Justice Baker's opinion that the case was not ripe for judicial review.

name: MIKE MCGRATH
description: Concurred, argued that the Attorney General wrongly applied an appropriation restriction to a constitutional amendment initiative.

name: JIM RICE
description: Concurred, authored the majority opinion affirming the lower court's decision on all three issues.

name: BETH BAKER
description: Concurred, but argued that the Batson framework for reviewing peremptory challenges should be revisited to provide greater protection against discriminatory practices, consistent with the Montana Constitution's Dignity and Equal Protection Clauses, and to account for implicit bias.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the facial challenge to HB 286 was ripe but failed on its merits because the statute's plain language does not establish a presumption against State ownership or deprive Advocates of a constitutionally protected interest, and the denial of the motion to amend was not an abuse of discretion as the proposed amendment would not present a definite, concrete injury.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred, argued that the private gathering of committee members, lacking a quorum, was not a formal public meeting subject to open meeting laws or the constitutional right to public access, distinguishing it from previous cases involving more formally structured bodies.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the Court's decision creates a judicial exception to the public's constitutional right to know, undermines the intent for open government, and that purposefully excluding members to avoid a quorum violates the constitutional right to know.

name: Dirk Sandefur
description: Concurred, argued that the warrantless search was lawful under the probation search exception and the exclusionary rule did not apply to the manner of entry or detention.

name: Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that while troubled by the officers' treatment of Peoples, affirming the decision was necessary due to precedent on the exclusionary rule.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, argued that Peoples's constitutional rights were violated by the unreasonable search and the evidence should have been suppressed.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that Peoples's constitutional rights were violated by the unreasonable search and the evidence should have been suppressed.

name: JIM RICE, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the initial entry into the driveway was permissible due to the officer's uncertainty about the property's ownership and Smith's flight, but further warrantless investigation became improper once Smith asserted his privacy rights and his residency was confirmed.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the subpoenas were impermissibly overbroad, exceeded legislative authority, and sought confidential information, violating separation of powers and privacy rights.

name: DIRK M. SANDEFUR
description: Concurred, argued that the constitutional doctrine of separation of powers limits legislative authority and prevents one branch from encroaching on another, which is crucial for constitutional democracy.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, argued that quashing the subpoenas was mandated by the constitutional doctrine of separation of powers, as the Legislature was investigating purported judicial misconduct, which is not a valid legislative purpose and interferes with an independent branch of government.

name: Dirk Sandefur
description: Concurred, argued that Staker had a subjective expectation of privacy but it was not objectively reasonable in society, thus no constitutional search occurred.

name: Justice James Jeremiah Shea
description: Concurred, arguing that SB 140 is constitutional as it aligns with the Framers' intent for judicial selection, which did not mandate a commission and allowed legislative discretion, and that the new process provides sufficient vetting.

name: JIM RICE, J.
description: Concurred, but wrote separately to address the extraordinary and extraconstitutional actions taken by the Legislature and Department of Justice during the proceeding, which he viewed as contemptuous and destructive to the democratic system.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, arguing that SB 140 is unconstitutional because it fails to provide a merit-based selection process for judicial nominees as intended by the Framers, thereby allowing direct gubernatorial appointments and threatening judicial independence.

name: Justice Beth Baker
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court's errors in admitting the forensic interview were harmless and that the GPS monitoring statute is facially constitutional.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred, delivering the majority opinion that affirmed the defendant's convictions, finding the Privacy in Communications statute constitutional and correctly applied.

name: Dirk Sandefur
description: Concurred, argued that "legal demands" in MWUA do not include MWQA nondegradation standards, and the MWUA's objection limitations do not violate constitutional environmental rights because other statutes provide adequate remedies.

name: Laurie McKinnon
description: Dissented, argued that the Court's interpretation of MWUA's "legal demands" is incorrect, that DNRC should consider water quality and dewatering effects on Outstanding Resource Waters (ORWs) when issuing permits, and that the majority's ruling undermines the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment.

name: Ingrid Gustafson
description: Dissented, argued that the Court's interpretation of MWUA's "legal demands" is incorrect, that DNRC should consider water quality and dewatering effects on Outstanding Resource Waters (ORWs) when issuing permits, and that the majority's ruling undermines the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment.

name: Justice Ingrid Gustafson
description: Concurred, argued that the District Court erred by not considering rehabilitation evidence when determining if Keefe was irreparably corrupt, but did not err in denying Keefe his own expert or a jury trial for incorrigibility.

name: Chief Justice Mike McGrath
description: Concurred with reversing the resentencing but dissented from remanding for another sentencing, arguing that the Montana Constitution warrants stronger protection for youthful defendants and that life without parole for juveniles should be presumed unconstitutional unless proven otherwise.

name: Justice Dirk Sandefur
description: Concurred that the District Court erred in not considering rehabilitation evidence and that Keefe had no right to his own expert or a jury trial, but dissented from remanding for resentencing, arguing the State failed to prove Keefe was irreparably corrupt and the parole restriction should simply be struck.

name: Justice Laurie McKinnon
description: Concurred on Issues One and Three (expert and jury trial) but dissented on Issue Two, arguing that Keefe received an individualized resentencing where youth characteristics were considered, and the sentence was not disproportionate.

name: Justice Jim Rice
description: Concurred and dissented with Justice McKinnon's opinion.
